prompt: Name one of the seven symbols used in Roman numerals.
source: The seven classical Roman numeral symbols: I, V, X, L, C, D, M.
valueLogic: I, V and X are produced instantly by almost anyone. C and L take a moment. M is known but often forgotten in the list. D is the genuine tail - most players never reach it, which is exactly the gradient the primes round lacked.
note: Single-letter names and numeric aliases verified against the matcher: norm() keeps digits and single characters, and exact matching runs before any length-gated fuzzy step. No other round in the game uses digits.

answers.name: I
answers.fact: One. A single tally mark, and the origin of the whole system.

answers.name: V
answers.fact: Five. One theory: an open hand, thumb and fingers forming the V.

answers.name: X
answers.fact: Ten. Often explained as two Vs joined point to point - two hands.

answers.name: C
answers.fact: One hundred, from centum. The source of per cent and century.

answers.name: L
answers.fact: Fifty. Unlike C for centum or M for mille, it isn't the initial of its Latin word.

answers.name: M
answers.fact: One thousand, from mille - the root of mile, a thousand Roman paces.

answers.name: D
answers.fact: Five hundred. The symbol almost nobody produces unprompted, and the whole tail of this round.

distractors.name: N
distractors.note: Used by medieval scribes for nulla, zero - but not one of the seven classical symbols.

distractors.name: Zero
distractors.note: The Romans had no symbol for it, which is why the system is so awkward to calculate with.

distractors.name: IV
distractors.note: A combination of two symbols rather than a symbol itself.

distractors.name: MM
distractors.note: Two thousand - M repeated, not a separate symbol.

distractors.name: K
distractors.note: Not a Roman numeral. A modern shorthand for thousand.
